title: Why Bigger Context Windows Don't Solve Everything
use_cases: Use when evaluating the trade-offs between massive context windows and RAG architectures
Configure when processing documents exceeding 100,000 tokens
Implement when maintaining factual consistency is critical for long-form content generation
Use when optimizing for system latency and hardware constraints in local LLM deployments
content:
You might think the solution is obvious: just use an AI model with a massive context window. Some models now offer 200,000+ tokens. In theory, you could fit a large novel into a single context window.

But there are problems with that approach.

First, cost. Sending 150,000 words to an AI model with every generation request gets expensive fast. You're paying for those tokens every single time.

Second, speed. Processing massive context windows is slow. The AI has to parse all that text before it can start generating.

Third, hardware. Running local models with huge context windows requires enormous amounts of VRAM. Most people don't have that kind of hardware.

And here's something I learned that surprised me: even with a 200,000-token context window, AI models still make mistakes with details buried deep in the context. If a character's eye color was mentioned once, 100,000 words ago, and never came up again, the AI might forget it or get it wrong. The context is there, but finding and using that one detail correctly isn't guaranteed.

Large context windows help, but they don't solve the consistency problem completely.

When I started developing AI Story Stream, I knew I had to solve this. Authors write long-form fiction. Novels are 80,000 to 120,000+ words. If my app couldn't handle that length with good consistency, it wouldn't be worth building.

I needed to give the AI a way to remember earlier parts of the story, even when those parts fell outside the context window.

That's where RAG came in.
